description: Regulatory T cells keep immune responses from turning on self tissue, and their identity is set by a transcriptional circuit in which RUNX1 and FOXP3 control Treg development. RUNX1, acting with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, drives transcription of FOXP3 itself; FOXP3 protein then binds back to the RUNX1:CBFB complex and redirects it. Inflammatory effector genes such as IL2 and IFNG, which RUNX1 would otherwise switch on, are repressed, while the surface hallmarks of the suppressive lineage are induced: the IL-2 receptor alpha chain, CTLA4 and GITR, with NFATC2 cooperating at these promoters. RUNX1:CBFB also activates the complement receptor CR1, whose appearance on activated T cells favours Treg generation. Loss of FOXP3 abolishes this programme and produces fatal multi-organ autoimmunity, and weakened Treg output underlies autoimmune disease and allergy more broadly.

RUNX family transcription factors cross-regulate one another, and here RUNX3 acts on the RUNX1 gene itself: bound with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX3 occupies Runx response elements in the distal P1 promoter of RUNX1 and represses its transcription. This negative feedback sets the balance between two related master regulators whose combined output shapes haematopoietic stem cell emergence, lymphocyte and megakaryocyte differentiation, and gut epithelial homeostasis. Because neither factor binds DNA efficiently alone, the shared non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB determines how much of either complex is available, and shifting occupancy of the P1 promoter changes which RUNX1 isoform predominates. Loss of this restraint matters clinically: RUNX1 dosage is sensitive, its disruption underlies familial platelet disorder and recurrent leukaemic translocations, while RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers.

The Hippo pathway effectors YAP1 and its paralogue WWTR1 (TAZ) drive growth-promoting transcription by partnering with TEAD family DNA-binding factors, and one of their canonical outputs is CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor), a matricellular protein that fuels proliferation, matrix production and fibrosis. RUNX3 acts here as a brake: by binding the TEAD:YAP1 complex it blocks its loading onto the CCN2 promoter, damping transcription of this growth factor. The interaction links a classical tumour-suppressor RUNX transcription factor to organ-size and contact-inhibition control, and helps explain why loss or silencing of RUNX3, common in gastric and other epithelial cancers, permits unrestrained YAP-driven target gene expression. The balance set at TEAD-bound enhancers thus determines whether epithelial cells proliferate and remodel their surroundings or remain quiescent, placing this regulation at the intersection of Hippo signalling, tissue repair and tumour suppression.

FOXO transcription factors drive programmes of stress resistance, autophagy, gluconeogenesis, apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and growth factor signalling switches those programmes off by moving the factors out of the nucleus. This is the main output of insulin and PI3K/AKT signalling onto metabolic and longevity gene expression: when insulin is present, hepatic glucose production and catabolic gene expression are suppressed, and when signalling is lost the factors return to chromatin. AKT1, AKT2 and AKT3 phosphorylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 at conserved sites, producing a conformational change that exposes a nuclear export signal; 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAB, YWHAZ and stratifin then bind the phosphorylated factors and hold them in the cytosol, away from their target promoters. FOXO6 lacks the export signal and stays nuclear, so phosphorylation instead dampens its transcriptional activity. Loss of this control contributes to insulin resistance and tumour suppression escape.

This is a tumour-suppressive transcriptional switch in which RUNX3, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, turns on p14-ARF from the CDKN2A locus and so raises the barrier to oncogenic transformation. p14-ARF sequesters MDM2 and stabilises p53, meaning that loss of this arm allows cells carrying activating lesions such as mutant KRAS to proliferate instead of arresting or dying; RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers. The control is acetylation-dependent: the acetyltransferase p300 modifies RUNX3, acetylated RUNX3 is read by the bromodomain protein BRD2, and this complex drives p14-ARF transcription. Cyclin D1 opposes the response by delivering the deacetylase HDAC4 to RUNX3, stripping the mark and muting induction, which couples the output to cell cycle state. TGF-beta signalling feeds into the same node, linking growth-inhibitory cues to p53 pathway activation.

MECP2 reads methylated DNA and tunes neuronal gene expression, and the layers that set how much of it is present and what it does are the subject here. Loss or misdosage of MECP2 causes Rett syndrome, so the controls on its level and activity matter as much as the protein itself. Its mRNA is silenced post-transcriptionally by miR-132 acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes, placing MECP2 downstream of activity-dependent neurotrophin signalling. Activity also acts directly: calcium-dependent kinases including CaMK IV and PKA, along with HIPK2 and AURKB, phosphorylate MECP2 at distinct sites that shift its chromatin association and its choice of partner. Through those partners MECP2 can repress, via the NCoR/SMRT and SIN3A complexes with HDAC1/2, or activate together with CREB1. Interactions with FOXG1, huntingtin and the lamin B receptor further shape its function and nuclear positioning.

NPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor made in neurons after depolarisation, where it shapes the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses onto a cell; because its protein must appear quickly and disappear again, how much of its mRNA is translated is tightly controlled. Here that control is exerted by microRNAs acting on the unusually conserved NPAS4 3'UTR, with miR-224 and miR-203 among the species shown to repress reporter expression through it. Silencing is carried out by the RNA-induced silencing complex: an Argonaute protein loaded with the guide microRNA, scaffolded by a GW182-family partner (TNRC6A, TNRC6B or TNRC6C) that recruits deadenylation and decay machinery, with the RNA helicase MOV10 assisting on structured targets. Loss of this restraint disturbs experience-driven synaptic scaling, memory formation and seizure thresholds.

The transcription factor RUNX3 acts as a brake on NOTCH signalling, and losing that restraint is one route by which liver cells become tumorigenic. RUNX3 works at two points. It occupies the promoter of JAG1 and represses transcription of this NOTCH ligand, lowering the signal available to neighbouring cells. It also joins the coactivator complex assembled on cleaved NOTCH1 intracellular domain with RBPJ, Mastermind-like proteins and the acetyltransferases CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/KAT2B, and blocks activation of the target gene HES1. Because HES1 is a repressor that sustains progenitor states and blocks differentiation, this interference pushes cells toward differentiation and away from proliferation. RUNX3 silencing, common in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer, releases NOTCH output and links its tumour suppressor function directly to developmental cell-fate signalling.

Platelets arise from megakaryocytes, and the transcription factor RUNX1 with its partner CBFB sets the gene programme that makes them. The complex is induced as progenitors commit to the megakaryocytic lineage and switched off as they turn erythroid, and it cooperates with GATA1 and its partner ZFPM1 at megakaryocyte promoters. Which coregulators are recruited decides the outcome: arginine methylation by PRMT1 favours an activating complex with the acetyltransferases EP300 and KAT2B and WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes, whereas unmethylated RUNX1 binds SIN3A/SIN3B with HDAC1 and PRMT6 to repress. Targets include the integrin ITGA2B and GP1BA for adhesion and aggregation, THBS1, the alpha-granule chemokine PF4, MYL9, PRKCQ, NFE2 and NR4A3, plus MIR27A, which feeds back on RUNX1 translation. Loss of RUNX1 function causes familial platelet disorder with thrombocytopenia and predisposition to leukaemia.

RUNX2 is the master transcription factor of osteoblast differentiation, but the same factor also drives a migratory and invasive gene programme in bone and in tumour cells that colonise it. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 turns on ITGA5, which mediates attachment to fibronectin and helps breast cancer cells adhere within bone, ITGBL1, which modulates TGF-beta signalling and contributes to RUNX2-driven bone metastasis, and MMP13, a collagenase that degrades fibrillar collagen during skeletal remodelling and permits immune cells and cancer cells to move through matrix. AKT kinases phosphorylate RUNX2 and raise its transcriptional output, linking growth factor and PI3K signalling to this migratory programme. The same targets support endothelial cell movement during retinal angiogenesis and stem cell migration, so the pathway spans normal tissue morphogenesis and metastatic invasion.

MECP2 is a methyl-CpG-binding nuclear protein that tunes neuronal gene expression, and one of its outputs is the level of other transcriptional regulators. By acting on the promoters of factors such as CREB1 and MEF2C, together with the splicing regulator RBFOX1 and the nuclear receptor PPARG, it sets the transcriptional tone for activity-dependent neuronal maturation, synapse refinement and dendritic complexity. MECP2 can both repress and activate these targets depending on context, so its loss does not silence a single gene but shifts a whole regulatory layer. That dependency explains why MECP2 mutation causes Rett syndrome, in which early development appears normal before acquired speech and motor skills regress, and why duplication of the locus is equally damaging. The PPARG link extends its reach beyond neurons to adipocyte differentiation and metabolic gene programmes.

The transcription factor RUNX2, best known for driving osteoblast commitment, also acts on genes of the myeloid programme, and this arm of its activity is captured by its control of galectin-3. Together with its paralogue RUNX1 and the shared non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises RUNX binding to DNA and is required for its transcriptional output, RUNX2 stimulates transcription of LGALS3. Galectin-3 is present in myeloid progenitors and accumulates as those cells mature, contributing to adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammatory responses. Because the same RUNX-CBFB module governs haematopoietic differentiation more broadly, misregulation here links lineage-specifying transcription to disease: galectin-3 is abundantly expressed in pituitary tumours and glioma, and RUNX1-CBFB disruption is a recurrent event in leukaemia. The pathway therefore connects a core developmental transcription complex to the maturation state and secreted lectin output of myeloid cells.

RUNX1 is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and the many layers that set its abundance and activity determine whether hemogenic endothelium yields hematopoietic stem cells and whether progenitors mature into T cells, megakaryocytes and other lineages; dosage matters so much that haploinsufficiency causes familial platelet disorder with leukemia predisposition, and translocations disrupting the gene drive acute myeloid leukemia. Transcription proceeds from two alternative promoters used differently across development, while a panel of microRNAs including miR-17, miR-20a, miR-18a and miR-27a engage the 3'UTR through Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing complexes to limit translation. Protein activity is then tuned by partners and modifications: heterodimerization with CBFB is required for DNA binding and transactivation, D-type cyclins and CDK6 antagonize that step, SRC-family tyrosine phosphorylation is reversed by the phosphatase PTPN11, and PML directs subnuclear localization.

The AP-2 transcription factors TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C control a battery of growth factor and receptor genes, and through them the proliferative behaviour of epithelial and placental cells. Their targets read as a map of breast cancer biology: the estrogen receptor ESR1, the receptor tyrosine kinases ERBB2, EGFR and KIT, and the ligand TGFA are all directly stimulated, while VEGFA transcription is repressed, linking these factors to angiogenic output as well as to mitogenic signalling. Cooperating partners modulate the response, with YY1 association raising the rate of ERBB2 transcription and the bromodomain coactivator ATAD2 contributing to target gene activation. In placenta the same factors drive both chorionic gonadotropin subunits, supporting trophoblast hormone production. Overexpression of TFAP2C in estrogen-receptor-positive breast and endometrial tumours makes this circuitry a determinant of hormone-responsive tumour phenotype.

Inhibitory neurotransmission depends on a steady supply of GABA, and the methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 helps set that supply by directly and positively driving transcription of the two glutamate decarboxylase genes, GAD1 and GAD2, whose products convert glutamate to GABA. This link places MECP2, a reader of DNA methylation that tunes neuronal gene expression, upstream of the excitation-inhibition balance of cortical and subcortical circuits. Loss of MECP2 from GABA-releasing neurons lowers GABA content and reproduces much of the Rett syndrome phenotype, including breathing irregularity, stereotypies and motor and social deficits, while its loss specifically in parvalbumin interneurons blunts sensory-evoked responses and impairs motor learning along with maturation of interneuron membrane properties and expression of parvalbumin, GABA-A receptor subunits and potassium channels. The pathway thus connects epigenetic transcriptional control to inhibitory circuit function and neurodevelopmental disease.

FOXO transcription factors act as the nuclear output of insulin and growth factor signalling, and this branch covers their direct control of oxidative stress defence, fuel metabolism and neuronal gene programmes. When insulin is low, as in fasting, PI3K/AKT no longer restrains FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6, which then drive hepatic gluconeogenesis through PCK1 and G6PC1 while repressing glucokinase via a SIN3A:HDAC corepressor complex and repressing SREBF1 to hold back lipogenesis; IGFBP1 and resistin further tune systemic insulin sensitivity. In hypothalamic neurons the same factors raise the orexigenic peptides NPY and AGRP and repress POMC, linking nutrient status to appetite. Antioxidant targets SOD2 and catalase, with contributions from cofactors such as PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3, limit superoxide and peroxide burden and support neuronal survival in neurodegeneration. FOXO6 also induces PLXNA4 during cortical radial glia migration, and FBXO32 and TRIM63 induction underlies starvation-induced muscle wasting.

NPAS4 is an activity-induced transcription factor that couples neuronal excitation to changes in gene expression, and through it to the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses on a stimulated neuron. It matters for experience-dependent plasticity, contextual memory formation, protection of neurons after seizure or ischaemic injury, and for insulin gene expression in stressed pancreatic beta cells. Because its basic helix-loop-helix domain cannot bind DNA alone, NPAS4 dimerizes with ARNT, ARNT2 or BMAL1 and recruits coactivators such as CREBBP, with MAPK1/MAPK3 signalling and nuclear export machinery shaping its activity and short half-life. Target genes span neuronal differentiation and maturation (CDK5 with its activator CDK5R1, RBFOX3, RET), synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission (BDNF, IQSEC3, PLK2, SYT10, FOS), and metabolic and circadian outputs including NAMPT. It is also expressed in endothelium, where it has been linked to angiogenesis.

TGF-beta can instruct a cell to die rather than divide, and one route to that outcome is transcriptional induction of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. Here RUNX3 drives BCL2L11 transcription, acting on the gene's promoter together with receptor-activated SMAD3 and its partner SMAD4 and with the forkhead factor FOXO3. The BIM protein that results neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and promotes BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, committing the cell to the intrinsic apoptotic programme. This arm of TGF-beta signalling contributes to the cytokine's tumour-suppressive behaviour in epithelial and gastric tissue and to apoptotic culling in lymphocytes; RUNX3 silencing by promoter methylation, or loss of SMAD signalling, removes this death output and allows cells that should have been eliminated to survive. It links growth factor signal transduction directly to the apoptotic machinery.

RUNX3 is a transcription factor that acts as a tumour suppressor in epithelial tissues and directs lymphocyte and dendritic cell differentiation, and the control of its expression and activity determines how much of it is available in the nucleus at any time. Its loss, most often through methylation of a CpG island at the internal promoter or through hypoxia-driven silencing, is a recurrent event in gastric and other solid tumours. Transcription responds to TGF-beta/SMAD input and to autoregulation; alternative promoter use and splicing yield isoforms differing in Runt-domain function. Once made, RUNX3 must heterodimerise with CBFB to bind DNA and recruits the acetyltransferase EP300 to activate targets such as CDKN2A. Activity is curtailed by SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation, which blocks nuclear entry, and by polyubiquitination via MDM2, SMURF1 and SMURF2 followed by proteasomal degradation, the reason the 26S proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes feature here.

When growth factor and insulin signalling wane, FOXO transcription factors escape cytoplasmic sequestration and enter the nucleus to shut down proliferation, and their transcription of cell cycle genes is how that arrest is enacted. FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 induce the CDK inhibitors p21 (CDKN1A) and p27 (CDKN1B), the pocket protein RBL2/p130 that helps maintain quiescence, the anti-proliferative genes CCNG2 and BTG1, GADD45A, caveolin-1, and KLF4. The output is withdrawal into G0 rather than division, a brake on erythroid progenitors, lymphocytes and neuroepithelial progenitors of the developing telencephalon, where FOXG1 opposes this arrest. TGF-beta input converges here: activated SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 partners with FOXO to drive p21 and, in muscle, myostatin, coupling cytostasis to differentiation. Loss of this arm of FOXO activity removes a tumour-suppressive restraint on growth factor-driven proliferation and stem cell exhaustion.

RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, is a lineage-defining transcription factor best known in blood development, and part of what it does is set the level of WNT signalling by transcribing WNT pathway components directly. This matters because the strength of WNT input decides whether progenitors self-renew or differentiate, and because RUNX1 is a recurrent target of translocation and mutation in leukaemia and a modifier of breast cancer behaviour. Two targets illustrate opposite arms of the same control. With the regulatory T cell factor FOXP3 as cofactor, the complex drives RSPO3, a secreted R-spondin that potentiates WNT receptor signalling and has oncogenic activity in breast tissue. With ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha, it instead induces AXIN1, a scaffold of the destruction complex that restrains beta-catenin. Hormonal and immune context therefore determines whether RUNX1 amplifies or dampens WNT output.

RUNX2 is the master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation and bone formation, and this pathway covers how much of it is made and how active it is once made. The dosage matters clinically: loss of one functional copy causes cleidocranial dysplasia, with defective clavicles and delayed cranial suture closure, while sustained activity drives skeletal mineralization and chondrocyte maturation. Transcription is driven from two alternative promoters, stimulated by estrogen receptor alpha, the homeodomain factors DLX5 and DLX6, and TWIST1, and repressed by the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, MSX2 and NKX3-2; estrogen-related receptor alpha switches between activation and repression depending on whether PGC1-alpha or PGC1-beta is bound. Protein-level control adds heterodimerization with CBFB and cooperation with cofactors, cytoplasmic sequestration by unphosphorylated STAT1, and polyubiquitination by SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2-containing cullin-RING ligases followed by proteasomal degradation.

Osteoblasts are made, not born, and RUNX2 acting with its partner CBFB is the transcriptional switch that commits mesenchymal progenitors to the bone-forming lineage and drives the genes that build mineralized matrix. Loss of this programme gives cleidocranial dysplasia and failed ossification, while its output — type I collagen, osteocalcin, and the cartilage-associated matrix protein UCMA — defines the skeleton's organic scaffold and its endocrine activity. RUNX2 cooperates with SP7 (Osterix) and SATB2 at target promoters, and is tuned by a dense layer of regulation: MAPK phosphorylation and SRC/YES1-dependent YAP1 binding respectively promote and restrain activity at the osteocalcin promoter, activated androgen receptor and HDAC recruitment block DNA binding, Notch effectors HEY1 and HES1 and the zinc finger ZNF521 repress it, and ubiquitin-dependent turnover limits its abundance. The pathway sits at the junction of skeletal development, hormonal signalling and matrix production.

Growth arrest imposed by TGF-beta depends on turning on the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, and RUNX3-driven transcription of CDKN1A is one route by which that happens. It matters most in gastric and other epithelia, where loss of this control removes a brake on proliferation: mice lacking Runx3 become insensitive to TGF-beta and develop gastric epithelial hyperplasia, and RUNX3 silencing is a recurrent event in gastric cancer. Mechanistically, TGFB1 signalling activates a SMAD3:SMAD4 complex that RUNX3 binds and cooperates with at the CDKN1A promoter; the RUNX3 heterodimer also engages the tumour suppressor ZFHX3 to reinforce induction. RUNX3 can additionally act as a co-factor for TP53, boosting p53-dependent target genes including CDKN1A, linking this transcriptional node to both cytokine-driven and damage-driven cell cycle arrest.

B cells need a functioning antigen receptor signalling apparatus, and part of that apparatus is put in place transcriptionally before any antigen is ever seen. Here RUNX1 controls transcription of genes acting in B cell receptor signalling, most directly the B lymphoid tyrosine kinase BLK, which propagates receptor engagement into the intracellular kinase cascades that drive B cell development, differentiation and antibody responses. RUNX1 works as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises DNA binding, and cooperates at the BLK promoter with the ETS-family factors ELF1 and ELF2 and with PAX5, the transcription factor that commits and maintains the B lymphoid lineage. This convergence of lineage-determining and general ETS regulators on a single kinase gene illustrates how haematopoietic transcription factors specify signalling competence; RUNX1 itself is a recurrent target of leukaemic translocation and mutation.

Retinoic acid pushes cells out of cycle and into differentiation, and part of how it does so is by shutting down genes that support growth. In this arm of the response, the transcription factor TFAP2A accumulates after retinoic acid treatment and acts as a repressor rather than an activator, partnering with the nucleolar chaperone nucleophosmin (NPM1) at target promoters. The repressed targets are growth- and proliferation-associated: the mitochondrial chaperonin HSPD1, the rRNA methyltransferase NOP2, and the cell cycle transcription factor MYBL2, the latter two used as proliferation markers. Repression is thought to work through NPM1-dependent recruitment of the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, deacetylating promoter chromatin. The complex also occupies the NPM1 promoter itself, consistent with the fall in NPM1 levels after treatment, giving a self-limiting loop that links retinoid signalling to withdrawal from proliferation.

The transcription factor RUNX1, working with its obligate partner CBFB, directs the haematopoietic gene programme, and part of that programme is the cell's ability to send and receive interleukin-family signals. Through this arm of its output RUNX1 turns on the gene for the leukemia inhibitory factor receptor, which transmits signals from an interleukin-6 family cytokine and contributes to blood cell production, embryo implantation, placental development and neural differentiation. Together with the ETS-family co-activator ELF1, the RUNX1:CBFB heterodimer also drives transcription of interleukin-3, a growth factor for multipotent progenitors and myeloid lineages. Because cytokine responsiveness and proliferative signalling are set here, disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB — as happens in familial platelet disorder and in the recurrent translocations of acute leukaemia — leaves progenitors with a miscalibrated response to interleukin cues.

The AP-2 family of transcription factors controls gene programmes in neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and placental development, and their loss produces recognizable malformation syndromes — branchio-oculo-facial syndrome from TFAP2A mutation, Char syndrome from TFAP2B — while TFAP2C is a driver of trophoblast and germ cell identity and is co-amplified with HER2 in breast cancer. Activation of these factors begins with dimerization through the helix-span-helix motif and binding of a basic region to palindromic GC-rich elements, though individual members prefer variant sites. Transactivation depends on partners: CITED family co-factors, CITED2 most avidly, dock on the helix-span-helix domain and bring in the acetyltransferase co-activators EP300 and CREBBP, and YEATS4 raises TFAP2B DNA binding, whereas WWOX sequesters AP-2 proteins and dampens their output. Mouse CITED2 loss recapitulates neural crest, cardiac and adrenal defects expected from failed AP-2 activation.

RUNX3 acts as a brake on WNT-driven proliferation, and its loss helps explain why this transcription factor behaves as a tumour suppressor in gastrointestinal epithelium. When WNT signalling stabilises beta-catenin, the protein enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF factors such as TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 to switch on growth-promoting target genes, chief among them cyclin D1 and MYC, which together push cells through the G1 restriction point. RUNX3 binds the beta-catenin:TCF/LEF complex directly and prevents it from occupying the CCND1 and MYC promoters, so the transcriptional output of the pathway is attenuated without blocking beta-catenin stabilisation itself. Silencing or mislocalisation of RUNX3 therefore leaves these complexes free to drive proliferation, linking this regulatory step to epithelial growth control and to carcinogenesis in the stomach and colon.

FOXO transcription factors decide whether a stressed cell mounts an antioxidant and repair response, arrests its cycle, or dies, and acetylation is one of the switches that sets that choice. Under oxidative stress the acetyltransferases CBP, p300 and PCAF add acetyl groups to FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, shifting which target promoters they favour and altering their nuclear retention in a way that can override the phosphorylation-driven nuclear exclusion imposed by insulin and growth factor signalling. The NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT3 reverse these marks, linking FOXO output to cellular energy and redox state; thioredoxin and its inhibitor TXNIP tie the same factors to the thiol redox environment. Through this regulation FOXO proteins govern stress resistance, metabolic adaptation, muscle atrophy programmes and tumour suppression, and the axis is central to how longevity signalling is interpreted at the level of gene expression.

Estrogen-responsive gene expression in breast epithelium is shaped not only by the hormone receptor itself but by the transcription factors it recruits, and RUNX1 acting on estrogen receptor mediated transcription is one such partnership. RUNX1, together with its obligate cofactor CBFB, binds directly to ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha and co-occupies the regulatory regions of a subset of estrogen target genes, among them the glycerolipid synthesis enzyme GPAM, the substrate adaptor KCTD6, and the Wnt pathway scaffold AXIN1. This gives RUNX1 a say in which genes respond to estrogen, linking hormone signalling to lipid metabolism and Wnt regulation rather than to proliferation alone. The relationship matters clinically: RUNX1 is a recurrently altered tumour suppressor in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and high GPAM expression tracks with better overall survival.

Myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow must be instructed to become granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes or platelet-producing megakaryocytes, and RUNX1 is the transcription factor that issues much of that instruction. Acting as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, it occupies target promoters and recruits the acetyltransferase CREBBP to open chromatin and drive transcription. Among the genes switched on are CSF2, encoding GM-CSF, a cytokine that supports growth, survival and maturation across several myeloid lineages; LGALS3, whose galectin-3 product rises as myeloid cells mature; and PRKCB, a protein kinase C isoform governing myeloid cell apoptosis. Because this programme sets the balance between progenitor self-renewal and differentiation, loss or translocation of RUNX1 or CBFB stalls maturation and is a recurrent cause of acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorders.

The methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 sets the transcriptional tone of maturing neurons, and one arm of that control is the direct regulation of the receptors, channels and transporters through which neurons sense and respond to their surroundings. Loss of MECP2 function causes Rett syndrome, in which apparently normal early development gives way to regression, and duplication of the gene is equally damaging, so the dosage of these target genes matters. Targets here include the AMPA receptor subunit GRIA2 and NMDA receptor subunits GRIN2A and GRIN2B, which shape excitatory synaptic transmission and its developmental switch; opioid receptors OPRK1 and OPRM1; the receptor tyrosine kinase MET and NOTCH1; the cation channel TRPC3 and glucose transporter SLC2A3. MECP2 acts with CREB1 and, through SIN3A and the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, can repress as well as activate. Tyrosine phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN4 provide indirect control of receptor kinase signalling.

RUNX3 is a transcription factor that shapes immune cell identity and the adhesion machinery leukocytes need to leave the bloodstream. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, it drives development of tissue-resident innate lymphoid cells of the ILC1 and ILC3 lineages, which guard mucosal surfaces against pathogens, by inducing the nuclear receptor RORC. In parallel it activates the integrin genes ITGAL (CD11a) and ITGA4 (CD49d), which mediate transendothelial migration during immune and inflammatory responses and provide co-stimulation to T cells. A shorter RUNX3 isoform lacking the DNA-binding Runt domain cannot transactivate these targets and accumulates as monocyte-derived dendritic cells mature, dampening inflammatory gene output. RUNX3 also raises expression of osteopontin (SPP1), a matrix protein that promotes invasiveness, linking this programme to pancreatic cancer progression as well as to normal mucosal immunity and leukocyte trafficking.

Skin epithelium must balance stem cell maintenance against terminal differentiation, and the transcription factor RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, tilts that balance in keratinocytes by repressing a small set of target genes. One is the protease inhibitor SERPINB13, which restrains cathepsin-family proteases such as cathepsin L and V that participate in epidermal differentiation and desmosomal remodelling; its loss is common in head and neck cancers. RUNX1 also represses SOCS3 and SOCS4, the negative feedback inhibitors of JAK-STAT signalling, so removing them raises STAT3 activity. Sustained STAT3 output favours proliferation and self-renewal in hair follicle and epithelial stem cell compartments, which is why this circuit is implicated in tumour initiation and in squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. The pathway thus links lineage-specific transcriptional repression to cytokine signalling strength and protease balance in stratified epithelium.

RUNX1, partnered with CBFB, is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and its output depends heavily on which chromatin co-factors it brings to a promoter. Here RUNX1 is shown engaging partners whose net effect on target genes remains ambiguous, a state of affairs that matters because the same complex can activate or silence the same promoter depending on context. HIPK2 phosphorylates both RUNX1 and the acetyltransferase EP300 bound to the complex, and leukemia-associated CBFB mutations disrupt this modification. RUNX1:CBFB also associates with polycomb repressive complex 1 subunits, including RING1/RNF2 with CBX and PHC proteins, found at many RUNX1 targets acting as co-activators or co-repressors. Direct contacts with SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A recruit nucleosome remodelling. Casein kinase 2 subunits add further phosphorylation input, tying hematopoietic gene control to chromatin state.

Long bones form by endochondral ossification, in which cartilage is progressively replaced by bone, and the step at which chondrocytes stop proliferating and become hypertrophic is controlled by RUNX2. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 drives transcription of Indian hedgehog and of markers of the hypertrophic state such as type X collagen, coupling chondrocyte maturation to the parathyroid hormone-related peptide feedback loop that sets growth plate length. GLI2 transduces the hedgehog signal, while HDAC4 restrains RUNX2 activity and so delays hypertrophy; loss of this brake causes premature ossification, and loss of RUNX2 function blocks maturation and limb elongation. The same factor governs osteoblast differentiation, making it the shared switch for skeletal patterning, and its haploinsufficiency underlies cleidocranial dysplasia.

When growth factor and insulin signalling falls silent, FOXO transcription factors move into the nucleus and switch on genes that kill the cell. This FOXO-driven transcription of cell death genes prunes neurons deprived of nerve growth factor, eliminates enteric nervous system precursors that lack RET signalling, and underlies much of the tumour-suppressive character of FOXO proteins; PI3K/AKT activity in cancer keeps FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 out of the nucleus and blocks it. The induced targets are the apoptotic machinery itself: the BH3-only proteins BIM and PUMA, the death ligand FASLG, the transcriptional repressor BCL6, plus PINK1 and the kinase STK11. Coactivators CREBBP and EP300 and the trimeric NF-Y complex work with FOXO at these promoters, while CITED2 and the stress-induced factor DDIT3 modulate the response, tying nutrient and stress sensing to a decision to die.

Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent endothelial and epithelial cells and set how much solute can cross a barrier; here that barrier programme is placed under transcriptional control by RUNX1. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX1 binds the promoters of the genes for ZO-1, occludin and claudin-5 and raises their expression, so the scaffolding protein and the two integral junctional membrane proteins that form the seal are produced together. The relevance is barrier permeability: in brain endothelium these three products are core constituents of the blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier, and loss of RUNX1 output, as occurs when the microRNA miR-18a represses it, loosens the junctions and increases passage across the barrier in glioma. This links a transcription factor best known in haematopoiesis to endothelial barrier integrity and to the problem of drug delivery into tumours.

AP-2 transcription factors act high in developmental hierarchies, and one of their outputs is the control of other transcription factors that pattern the embryo. Here TFAP2A and TFAP2C, as homodimers and possibly heterodimers, cooperate with the transcriptional coactivator CITED2 to stimulate expression of PITX2, a homeodomain factor that establishes left-right asymmetry and directs outflow tract and valve formation in the developing heart. Because PITX2 sits downstream, loss of this input reproduces laterality defects and congenital cardiac malformations seen when CITED2 or the AP-2 factors are disrupted; TFAP2A mutation in humans also causes branchio-oculo-facial syndrome, reflecting the family's wider role in neural crest and craniofacial development. The relationship illustrates how a coactivator-dependent dimeric factor converts positional signals into a downstream regulatory programme rather than directly into structural gene expression.

AP-2 transcription factors set how strongly a cell brakes its own division by controlling the p21 cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor gene. Because p21 restrains CDK-cyclin complexes at the G1/S transition and is a principal effector of growth arrest and senescence, the balance struck here determines whether cells proliferate or pause, and it is frequently skewed in tumours. Two closely related family members act in opposition at the same locus: TFAP2A binds the CDKN1A promoter and activates it, while TFAP2C represses it, recruiting MYC together with the histone demethylase KDM5B, which strips activating methylation from promoter histones to shut transcription down. The result is a switch in which the relative abundance of the two paralogues, rather than an external signal, dictates p21 levels, linking developmental transcription factor programmes to cell cycle entry and to differentiation-associated exit from the cycle.

NPAS4 is a neuron-specific transcription factor induced within minutes of activity that tunes inhibitory synapse number onto excited neurons, and the control of NPAS4 gene transcription is how that homeostatic brake is set. Calcium entry during neuronal stimulation drives transcription, with SRF acting as an activity-dependent activator at the promoter and PI3K/AKT signalling contributing, while calcium-free KCNIP3 (DREAM) occupies the promoter and holds it silent in the resting state. REST keeps the gene off in non-neuronal cells and can act in either direction in neurons, limiting the duration of the response. Stress imposes a second layer: glucocorticoid-bound NR3C1 binds upstream response elements and represses induction, and histone deacetylase activity and promoter CpG methylation state further gate the locus. Loss of this regulation disturbs excitatory-inhibitory balance, memory formation, and stress-related and neurodegenerative processes in the hippocampus.

AP-2 family transcription factors drive programmes of neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and mammary development, and their output must be restrained as well as switched on; this pathway covers the mechanisms that damp AP-2 activity. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the AP-2 transactivation domain and block transcriptional activation, a brake whose loss in KCTD1 mutation causes scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects. SUMO conjugation through the E2 enzyme UBE2I attaches SUMO1 to TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, converting them into weaker activators and influencing epithelial differentiation and cancer stem cell traits in breast tumours. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C outside the nucleus, preventing it from reaching its targets. Together these controls set the dosage of AP-2 signalling, which matters because both excess and deficiency distort embryonic patterning and epithelial gene expression.

Blood formation requires stem cells to stop renewing themselves and commit to a lineage, and RUNX1, acting with its partner CBFB, is one of the transcription factors that makes that decision. Its best-defined target here is SPI1 (PU.1): RUNX1 brings the histone methyltransferase KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter and upstream regulatory element, depositing activating H3K4 trimethylation, and the resulting PU.1 expression restrains stem cell self-renewal while enabling myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also sits within a TAL1-containing complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB transcription, a configuration that in T-ALL promotes proliferation and blocks apoptosis. Proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes reflect the degradation that limits RUNX1 levels, ITCH and CDK7-containing kinase activity among its regulators. Loss or translocation of RUNX1 underlies familial platelet disorder and acute myeloid leukemia.

MECP2 is the methyl-CpG-binding protein whose loss causes Rett syndrome, and much of its neuronal function comes down to setting the expression level of secreted signalling molecules that shape synapses and circuit activity. Here it governs transcription of neuronal ligands: the neurotrophin BDNF, which supports synaptic maturation and activity-dependent plasticity; corticotropin-releasing hormone, tied to stress responsiveness and anxiety behaviour; the neuropeptide somatostatin, marking an inhibitory interneuron population; and the Notch ligand DLL1, which influences neural progenitor fate. MECP2 can act in either direction at these promoters, recruiting the SIN3A corepressor with HDAC1 to deacetylate histones and dampen transcription, or cooperating with CREB1 to drive activity-dependent expression. Because ligand dosage rather than presence is what is tuned, both loss and duplication of MECP2 produce neurodevelopmental disease, linking chromatin readout of DNA methylation to synaptic and neuroendocrine output.
